summary: This informational document describes how Apple's Back to My Mac service is implemented. It provides connectivity between devices for file sharing and screen sharing, and addresses single sign-on, secure communication, and service discovery.

plainLanguage.summary: Back to My Mac lets you reach your home computer from anywhere. This explains how Apple's version connects and finds your machines.

questions: how does back to my mac work
remote access to mac over internet
what is back to my mac
how does btmm survive ip address changes
subtitle: Apple's system for secure remote access to Mac computers through NATs and across IP address changes

tldr.problem: Users want to securely connect to their home or work computers from anywhere, but face challenges from Network Address Translators (NATs), dynamic IP addresses, and the need for reliable authentication.
tldr.mechanism: BTMM combines DNS for service discovery and address mapping, NAT-PMP for NAT traversal, IPv6 Unique Local Addresses as stable host identifiers, Kerberos for authentication, and IPsec for end-to-end encryption, all integrated into a single user-friendly service.
tldr.outcome: Users can connect to other Macs by name with a click, share files and control screens remotely, and maintain connections even when IP addresses change—all with strong encryption and authentication.

today: Back to My Mac was first implemented in Mac OS X 10.5 in October 2007 and remains in use. The service demonstrates how multiple IETF standards can be combined to solve practical networking challenges.

sections.title: Remote Access and the NAT Problem
sections.content:
Back to My Mac (BTMM) is Apple's service for connecting to Mac computers remotely. Users can perform file sharing and screen sharing among computers at home, work, or while traveling. BTMM addresses a core networking challenge: enabling connections when devices are behind Network Address Translators (NATs) and have dynamically changing IP addresses.

The service was first shipped with Mac OS X 10.5 in October 2007 and has evolved since. It integrates several existing protocols rather than inventing new ones: DNS for discovery, dynamic DNS updates to reflect address changes, NAT traversal, IPv6 Unique Local Addresses as permanent device identifiers, Kerberos for authentication, and IPsec for secure communication. The user experience is simple: log in with MobileMe credentials, and click on a remote Mac to connect.
sections.plainLanguage: When you travel, your laptop gets a new internet address. Your home Mac does too when your internet provider assigns it a new one. But BTMM gives each computer a permanent invisible address so they can always find each other, even when their real addresses change. And it locks everything so only you can see or control your machines.

sections.title: Service Discovery and Address Management
sections.content:
Every BTMM user is assigned a DNS subdomain under members.me.com (for example, alice.members.me.com), and names each computer within that domain (for example, myMacPro.alice.members.me.com). BTMM uses DNS-based Service Discovery (DNS-SD) and DNS resource records to encode reachability information. Each host stores two key pieces of information: its IPv6 Unique Local Address (ULA) in an AAAA record, and its current network location in an SRV record.

The SRV record is the clever part. For hosts on public networks, it points directly to their IP address and port. For hosts behind a NAT, it includes both the NAT's public IP address and the port that the NAT has opened for this host. When a host needs to reach another, it queries the SRV record to find the current location and the IPv6 address, then establishes a connection using that information.

When a device's network changes or a NAT reassigns a port, the device updates the DNS records dynamically. To avoid stale information, BTMM uses Dynamic DNS Update Leases (DDUL) to limit record lifetime, and it fetches updates immediately using DNS Long-Lived Queries (LLQ), which push change notifications from the server rather than requiring polling.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it like a directory service. Each Mac has two phone numbers: one invisible permanent one (IPv6 ULA) and one visible temporary one (the current network address). The directory is updated automatically whenever the Mac moves, so when you call your home Mac, you get the right number even though it changes.

sections.title: NAT Traversal with NAT-PMP
sections.content:
Network Address Translators block inbound traffic by default. BTMM uses NAT-PMP (NAT Port Mapping Protocol), a protocol designed for exactly this problem. When a BTMM host detects it is behind a NAT (by finding its address falls in the private ranges defined in RFC 1918), it sends a NAT-PMP request to the gateway asking to open an inbound port.

The NAT-PMP request goes to the default gateway on UDP port 5351 and includes the internal port the host wants to use. The NAT responds by either granting that port or assigning a different one. The host can request a specific port (helpful for recovery after restarts), but the NAT is not obligated to grant it. Port mappings have a default lifetime of 3600 seconds; the host renews them every 1800 seconds. If a mapping expires or the DHCP lease changes, the NAT automatically deletes it.

For hosts on public networks with no NAT, BTMM still uses NAT-PMP to detect that and proceed normally. For scenarios BTMM cannot handle—such as NAT-behind-NAT or subnets behind a NAT gateway where the host's default router is not the NAT—users simply cannot use the service; it is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: When your Mac is behind a router, the router blocks incoming connections. BTMM politely asks the router: 'Please open port X so people can reach me.' The router says yes and for how long. When the time is almost up, BTMM asks again. If the router reboots or you reconnect, BTMM asks again and the router remembers where to send traffic for that port.

sections.title: Authentication and Encryption
sections.content:
BTMM employs multiple layers of security. For authentication, it uses Kerberos, a single sign-on technology. When a user first signs in to MobileMe on a computer, the system automatically retrieves a digital certificate and private key from the local Key Distribution Center. When connecting to another computer, the client authenticates using the Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication in Kerberos (PKINIT) protocol with this certificate. After initial authentication, the user receives a ticket permitting access to the remote host (typically valid for 10 hours).

For DNS exchanges, BTMM protects dynamic DNS updates and LLQ queries using Transaction SIGnature (TSIG) authentication, which uses a shared secret key derived from the subscriber's MobileMe password. Each DNS message gets a computed HMAC-MD5 signature.

For data communication, BTMM wraps IPv6 packets in IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), then encapsulates the encrypted packets in a UDP/IP tunnel. This approach ensures end-to-end encryption even when both endpoints have public addresses and could theoretically communicate directly. The IPsec Security Associations use the stable IPv6 ULA addresses rather than temporary external IP addresses, so connections survive network changes. Key exchange is handled by IKE (Internet Key Exchange) in aggressive mode using the subscriber's Fully Qualified Domain Name as both identifier and pre-shared key.
sections.plainLanguage: First, you prove who you are using your MobileMe password and a certificate. Then you get a ticket that lasts several hours so you don't have to prove it again. When you send data, it is locked in three layers: first by IPsec, then put in a UDP tunnel, and the permanent invisible address is used so the tunnel doesn't break when you move.

sections.title: Status and Evolution
sections.content:
Back to My Mac was first implemented in Mac OS X 10.5. As documented in this RFC, BTMM continues to evolve over time. The core architecture has remained stable, demonstrating the viability of combining proven technologies—DNS, dynamic DNS, NAT-PMP, IPv6 ULA, Kerberos, and IPsec—into a cohesive remote access solution.

The service has been widely adopted by Mac users and remains a core part of Apple's ecosystem. The approach of using IPv6 ULA as a stable host identifier proved particularly successful, allowing the system to leverage existing IPv6 code and libraries rather than introducing new addressing schemes.

This document serves as a technical reference for how BTMM works as of the 10.5.x era, showing how multiple IETF standards can be integrated to provide a complete solution for the practical problems of host mobility, NAT traversal, and secure remote access.
sections.plainLanguage: Back to My Mac started with Mac OS X 10.5 and is still used today. It shows that you do not need to invent new network protocols—you can combine the ones that already exist to solve real problems that people actually have, like connecting to their computers from across the world.
